questions.question: Which row operation is elementary?
options: Replace one row by a nonzero multiple of another row.
Multiply one row by a scalar, which may be zero.
Add the same nonzero constant to every entry of a row.
Add a multiple of one row to a different row.

questions.question: Why must the scalar be nonzero when multiplying a row in an elementary row operation?
options: A zero multiple would make the system inconsistent.
Multiplication by zero would not be reversible.
Scaling by zero would turn the system into a homogeneous one.
Multiplying by zero is harmless but never simplifies anything.

questions.question: Why are elementary row operations used in Gauss-Jordan elimination?
options: They deliberately change the solution set to one that is easier.
They simplify the matrix while preserving the solution set.
They preserve the determinant, so invertibility can be read off.
They keep the coefficient matrix fixed and change only the right-hand side.

questions.question: When working with an augmented matrix, why must row operations include the last column?
options: The last column must always be kept fixed to preserve equivalence.
The last column changes only under row swaps, never under scaling.
Including it keeps the matrix square, as row operations require.
Each row is a whole equation, right-hand side included.

questions.question: Which operation would create a leading $1$ from the row $(4,8,-12)$?
options: $R\leftarrow 4R$
$R\leftarrow 0R$
$R\leftarrow R+4R$
$R\leftarrow \frac{1}{4}R$

questions.question: Use $R_2\leftarrow R_2+3R_1$ on $R_1=(1,-2,0)$ and $R_2=(-3,5,7)$. What is the new $R_2$?
Why can elementary row operations be viewed as a safe way to simplify a system?
options: Each step removes one variable from the system for good.
Each operation keeps each equation's own solution set unchanged.
Each operation has an inverse, so nothing is lost.
The result does not depend on the order of the operations.

questions.question: Why is replacing a row by the sum of itself and another row allowed, but replacing it by just another row is usually not?
options: Replacing a row by another row is just a row swap in disguise.
The second is fine too, provided the copied row is nonzero.
The first is reversible; the second can lose a row for good.
The second can be undone too, but it changes the right-hand side.

questions.question: Apply $R_1\leftrightarrow R_2$ and then $R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1$ to $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. What is the final second row?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}-3&-5\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&3\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: In one step, both computed from the old rows, a student replaces $\boldsymbol{R}_1$ by $\boldsymbol{R}_1-\boldsymbol{R}_2$ and $\boldsymbol{R}_2$ by $\boldsymbol{R}_2-\boldsymbol{R}_1$. What is wrong with this?
options: The new rows are negatives of each other, so an equation is lost and the solution set can grow.
Nothing: each replacement on its own is elementary, so doing both at once is too.
It goes wrong only when $\boldsymbol{R}_1=\boldsymbol{R}_2$; otherwise the new system is equivalent.
The replacements are fine, but they must not be applied to the right-hand sides.

questions.question: Which single elementary row operation undoes $\boldsymbol{R}_2\to\boldsymbol{R}_2-5\boldsymbol{R}_1$?
options: $\boldsymbol{R}_1\leftrightarrow\boldsymbol{R}_2$
$\boldsymbol{R}_2\to5\boldsymbol{R}_2$
$\boldsymbol{R}_1\to\boldsymbol{R}_1+5\boldsymbol{R}_2$
$\boldsymbol{R}_2\to\boldsymbol{R}_2+5\boldsymbol{R}_1$
